turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_retention_train.csv: 55 real samples, columns
    process/composition columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B,
    Al, Cu, W, S) and `target` (the measured hot-strength retention ratio
    YS(600C)/YS(20C)).
  - b3_htsteel_retention_pool.csv: 26 CANDIDATE samples whose hot-strength
    retention ratio YS(600C)/YS(20C) was NOT measured, columns
    `candidate_id` and the same process/composition columns.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST hot-
strength retention ratio YS(600C)/YS(20C), then select the 5 best candidates
from the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
## Reasoning from the training data

**What drives high YS(600 °C)/YS(20 °C) in the 55 training points?**

1. **γ′-strengthened Fe–Ni–Cr austenitics with Ti (+Al, +W)** — clearly the top of the training set:
 - Fe42/Cr15/**Ni36/Ti1.3/W3.15** → **1.00**
 - Fe41/Cr15/**Ni36.3/Ti0.78/Al1.09/W3.58** → **0.875**
 - Fe60/Cr11.25/**Ni23/Ti2.9/Al0.4**/Mo1.3 → **0.903**
 - Fe50/Cr15/**Ni26.9/Ti1.16/Al1.23/W2.97** → **0.821**
 So the combination **Ni > 19 % + Ti ≥ 0.8 % + Al** (A286 / Incoloy-type precipitation hardening) is the single strongest positive signal. Ti alone in a plain 18-8 (Ti 0.5–0.7, Ni 9–10) only gives 0.63–0.64, so Ni content matters together with Ti.

2. **High-Mn, high-V, high-C austenitics** (Mn 7–8, V 1.3–1.7): 0.80–0.88. Mn alone without V/C (plain austenitic 24Cr-16Ni-6Mn) is only 0.55, so it is the V + C carbide contribution, not Mn, that helps.

3. **Mo in ferritic/low-alloy steels** raises retention (0.5Cr–0.5Mo → 0.94; 1Cr–0.5Mo/V → 0.65–0.77; Mo-free plain C-Mn → 0.30–0.47). Nearest-neighbour logic therefore predicts a fairly high value for the 0.5Cr–0.5Mo pool member.

4. **Negatives**: Mo-free, Ti-free plain stainless (13Cr, 17Cr, 18-8, 21-6-9 duplex) sit at 0.29–0.52; plain C–Mn steels sit at 0.30–0.47; Cu-heavy/Mo-heavy austenitics without Ti/Al are mid-0.5s.

**Scoring the pool with these rules**

| candidate | key features | analogue in train | predicted |
|---|---|---|---|
| **c019** | Ni35, Ti2.8, Al1.05, W3.2, Cr15 | 1.00 / 0.875 samples | ~0.95 |
| **c011** | Ni19.5, Ti2.9, Al0.8, B0.02 | 0.903 sample | ~0.87 |
| **c013** | Ni27.5, Ti1.16, Al1.05, W2.4, Mo2.5 | 0.821 sample + W/Mo | ~0.85 |
| **c004** | Ni26, Ti1.2, Al1.2, Mo2.91 (no W) | 0.821 sample | ~0.82 |
| **c015** | 0.55Cr–0.5Mo, C0.125 | 0.9375 sample (near-duplicate) | ~0.80 (uncertain) |
| c003 | Mn14, Ni3.65, Ti0.5, no V | Mn-only austenitic ≈0.55–0.65 | ~0.65 |
| c018/c009/c002/c006/c016 | 18-8(+Ti) | 0.39–0.64 | ~0.55 |
| c001/c007/c022/c014/c024/c012/c025/c017 | Cr-Mo-V low alloy / 11Cr | 0.55–0.69 | ~0.6 |
| c000/c010/c020/c021/c023 | plain C-Mn, Mo-free, 17Cr | 0.30–0.49 | low |

The five clear winners are the Ni–Ti–Al precipitation-hardened grades, with the 0.5Cr–0.5Mo near-duplicate as the fifth pick.

**Final: c019, c011, c013, c004, c015**
